catalog_quote: In Zambian languages, in contrast, syllables are more or less evenly stressed, i.e. they are pronounced with almost the same degree of prominence or force. In some languages, however, (e.g. Cewa) the penultimate syllable seems to be pronounced with slightly greater force than the rest of the syllables in the same word. However, it must be remembered that that is also the syllable, according to the rule mentioned earlier, which is lengthened, so that the stress may be the effect of the lengthening of the vowel. In any case, independent of the lengthening of vowels, stress in Zambian languages does not distinguish words from each other in meaning. A characteristic feature of all Zambian languages is that each of their syllables carries tone. ... There are only two contrastive tones in Zambian languages, high and low, which serve to distinguish ... between words which are otherwise identical in all other respects.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Pan-Zambian generalisation (not Soli-specific): no contrastive word stress; syllables roughly equally prominent, with at most slight penultimate prominence in some languages attributable to penultimate vowel lengthening; every syllable bears H or L tone. Hachipola 1991 independently treats Soli as a two-tone Tonga lect (lexical and grammatical tone, citation-form data) and says nothing about stress. The Soli-specific primary phonology (van Eeden 1935/36) could not be opened.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the hedge that some languages (Cewa named) show slight penultimate prominence tied to penultimate lengthening; whether Soli is among them is not stated.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about 'Zambian languages' as a class, from the national language survey team (Soli was among the languages surveyed and is cited elsewhere in the chapter), i.e. word-level prominence in general terms; it is not a description of Soli and should not be catalogued as Soli's own statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Soli = Chisoli/Tjisoli, Guthrie M.62, Botatwe (Bantu Botatwe/'Tonga lects'); van Eeden's variety is 'Soli spoken in north-west Rhodesia' (fieldwork early 1930s, Beit Trust fellow); Hachipola's Soli informants were from Manyika and Chongwe (Lusaka Rural), i.e. the same soli1239; note a 'Soli-wa-Manyika' of Rufunsa is mentioned in Language in Zambia as a sub-variety. The quoted 1978 statement is pan-Zambian, not tied to any Soli dialect.

The section continues (lines 3196-3236, pp. 70-71): 'There are only tvvo contrastive tones in Zambian languages, high and low', with minimal pairs from Lunda, Lozi, Nyanja, Bemba and a remark on contextual tone lowering, so 'tone language with a stress statement' is the right label. The 'rule mentioned earlier' is the penultimate-lengthening rule at…
new_statements.relation_note: This is the same passage the existing statement was taken from (Kashoki & Mann 1978: 70); the verbatim scanned reading confirms it and adds the following sentences (stress possibly an effect of penultimate lengthening; stress never distinctive; every syllable carries tone, two contrastive tones). The catalog record for Soli has an empty rule; this source supports 'no distinctive word stress, tonal' as a generic Zambian-Bantu statement rather than a Soli-specific one. Soli appears in the book only in the census table (p. 21), the ch. 1 intelligibility discussion (p. 36), one imperative example 'Soli vona, vonani "see"' (p. 78) and Lehmann's ch. 3 lexicostatistics (pp. 102-113), none of which…
new_statements.rule_in_words: All Zambian languages (Soli among the languages surveyed) are two-tone languages in which every syllable carries tone; syllables are more or less evenly stressed, stress is not distinctive, and where a slightly stronger penultimate is heard (the authors' example is Cewa, not Soli) it may be only the effect of penultimate vowel lengthening. The statement is generic for 'Zambian languages'; Soli is never named in the stress or lengthening passages, and the penultimate-lengthening rule (pp. 63-64) is stated for Eastern Province and several North-Western Province languages, which does not cover Soli (Lusaka/Central).
new_statements.exceptions: Some languages (e.g. Cewa) show slightly greater force on the penultimate syllable, attributed possibly to the penultimate lengthening rule; stress never distinguishes words in meaning.
new_statements.identity_note: The stress statement is generic for 'Zambian languages' (Kashoki & Mann survey all Bantu languages of Zambia; Soli is listed in the census table on p. 21 and in Lehmann's Kafue Basin chapter as Bantu Botatwe, spoken east of Lusaka). Soli is not named in the stress passage; the penultimate-force remark is exemplified by Cewa (Nyanja), and the penultimate-lengthening rule on pp. 63-64 is attributed to Eastern Province and some North-Western Province languages, not to Soli's area.

sources.note: Generic statement for Zambian (Bantu) languages, Soli being one of the languages the survey covered (Soli verb forms cited p. 78): syllables are 'more or less evenly stressed'; in some languages (e.g. Cewa) the penult seems slightly stronger, probably an effect of penultimate vowel lengthening; stress never distinguishes words; every syllable carries tone (two tones, H and L). Nothing Soli-specific on stress.

sources.note: Silent on word stress. Ch. 2 gives vowel/consonant inventories and phonotactics for each lect incl. Soli; sec. 3.3 'Tone' (pp. 264ff.): tone is lexically and grammatically distinctive in the Tonga lects; for lects other than Plateau (incl. Soli) tone data are citation forms only, 'no variation has been observed within the core lects' in surface citation tone; Soli data were not tape-recorded (p. 39-40). Discusses Goldsmith's accentual reanalysis of Tonga tone, not stress.
